evidence_quotes.quote: Based on literature review, an ordered logit model was estimated to investigate whether household location (rural versus urban), sex of household head, main occupation of household head, literacy of household head, marital status and household income predict the level of a household on the drinking water ladder
That is, the odds of an urban household being on top level of basic services versus the combined levels of no access, unimproved, and limited are 5 times higher than that for a rural household.
The 1995 Act is very clear in limiting the jurisdiction of the five major water utility companies to only urban areas (Malawi Government, 1995).

raw_response.rationale: Full text (18 pages) read completely. The study surveys N = 535 households in Lilongwe, Malawi (262 in three high-density urban neighborhoods and 273 in villages around two rural trading centers) and reports genuine inferential statistics (chi-square tests in Tables 2-3, multivariate ordinal logistic regression on JMP drinking water ladder in Table 4, independent-samples t-test on collection time in Table 5, and binary logistic regression on 24-hour availability in Table 8). However, every inferential model tests only a coarse geographic indicator (Lilongwe urban vs. Lilongwe rural) alongside household socio-demographic predictors (sex of household head, farming vs. non-farm occupation, literacy, marital status, and monthly income). Affordability (Table 6: 12.36% urban vs. 1.75% rural monthly income spent on water) and perceived livelihood burdens (Table 9) are reported descriptively only (means and SDs). The rule-type legal and institutional mechanisms relevant to Criterion 2—specifically the Waterworks Act of 1995 restricting Water Boards' statutory jurisdiction to urban areas, Lilongwe Water Board's 2020-2025 full-cost recovery tariff policy, and the 62.2% vacancy rate in rural water institutions—are not measured or tested quantitatively and appear solely in an ex-post narrative discussion in Section 4.4 (p. 15) drawing on secondary documents. Because a generic urban-versus-rural geographic dummy confounds urbanization, population density, and physical infrastructure proximity with statutory utility jurisdiction, the tested quantitative exposure fails narrow Criterion 2 and does not yield a SWiM-eligible effect.
